_about: The Library's 'Save the Cat' shelf (src/pages/library.js, renderSaveTheCat). COPYRIGHT RULES, owner decision recorded in docs/WIP-EMOTION-PLAN.md: the book is copyrighted. This file teaches the GENERAL craft ideas in ORIGINAL wording. Short, widely used concept names are kept as labels (the fifteen beat names, the ten genre names, 'the Board', the names of the rules of thumb) together with widely known page-placement conventions for a 110-page script; everything else is described in fresh sentences. Never reproduce the book's text, sentences, chapter titles or order of argument, its descriptions of its own lists, or its film examples. Every example comes from the four studied films (dragon, 96, porthozhil, vikramvedha; src/data/studies.json) or src/data/films.json, labels the FUNCTION of a moment, retells no more plot than a clause and quotes no dialogue. The book is credited ONCE, in `credit`, as recommended reading. Never type the product's brand name here (npm run test:brand). The `studio` link points at the Story stage's Beat Sheet, where `save_the_cat` (src/data/frameworks.json) is a selectable beat sheet. Read-only content: no storage keys; each id is an anchor (#stc-...).

credit.title: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You’ll Ever Need
credit.author: Blake Snyder
credit.note: Recommended reading. This shelf is an independent summary of the general ideas the book is known for, written in our own words with Tamil and Indian examples of our own. It is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by the author, his estate or the publisher. Buy the book for the full text, its reasoning and its examples.

intro.lede: Know what your movie is before you write it, and be able to say so in one sentence that makes a stranger want to see it.
paragraphs: The book behind this shelf is a practical, commercially minded approach to screenwriting, and its starting point is that the idea comes first. Many writers begin with a scene, a character or a mood and discover the story while drafting. This approach turns that around: before a single page, you should be able to pitch the film in a line, know what kind of film it is, and see its whole shape on one wall. Writing pages before that work is done is how drafts end up running in circles.

Its tools fall into a few groups. A one-line pitch and a title that together tell an audience what they are buying. A way of thinking about genre by the engine of the story rather than its surface, so that a crime film and a comedy can turn out to share a skeleton. A beat sheet of fifteen moments, each with a job and an approximate page, that gives a feature its rhythm. A wall of index cards — the Board — on which the whole film is laid out and rearranged before drafting. And a set of rules of thumb, each a small, memorable warning about a way scripts commonly go wrong.

None of this is a formula for originality, and the approach is often criticised as producing look-alike films when it is followed mechanically. Used well, it is something more modest and more useful: a set of checks. It tells you where a draft sags, which moment is missing and whether the story you are telling is the story your opening promised. Indian cinema, with its interval and its tolerance for tonal mixture, bends the shape in places, and the mappings below say where.

pillars.label: Story first
pillars.text: Decide what the film is, for whom, and why they would buy a ticket, before you decide how a single scene plays.

pillars.label: One line, one title
pillars.text: If the premise cannot be pitched in a sentence with a title that hints at it, the concept is not finished yet.

pillars.label: Genre as engine
pillars.text: Classify by what drives the story, not by its setting, so you can learn from films that look nothing like yours.

pillars.label: Structure as rhythm
pillars.text: Fifteen beats at roughly known pages tell you when the audience expects a turn, so you can deliver or subvert it deliberately.

pillars.label: See it whole
pillars.text: Lay the film out as about forty cards on one board, fix it there, and only then write pages.

pillars.label: Rules of thumb
pillars.text: Short warnings about recurring mistakes, useful precisely because they are easy to remember while rewriting.

logline.title: The logline and the title
paragraphs: A logline is one sentence that says who the story is about, what happens to them and what makes it worth watching. It is the first test of a concept, not a marketing afterthought: if you cannot write a compelling one, it is usually because the idea itself is unclear or ordinary.

A strong logline has an inner contradiction that makes it interesting — a person placed in exactly the situation they are least equipped for, a goal that cuts against who they are. It lets the listener picture the film, it implies who the audience is and what the experience will feel like, and it hints at the stakes. The title should do some of the same work: tell the audience what kind of film this is and what is at its centre, without being a riddle that only makes sense after watching.

qualities.label: Irony
qualities.text: Look for the friction inside the premise: the cautious man forced to gamble, the cheat who must finally do the work. That contradiction is the hook.

qualities.label: A picture
qualities.text: A good logline makes a listener see the film — a setting, a situation, a face — and run a trailer in their head.

qualities.label: Audience and cost
qualities.text: It implies who will want to watch, roughly what scale of film it is, and therefore whether it can be made.

qualities.label: Stakes and a goal
qualities.text: It names what the protagonist is trying to do and what they lose if they fail.

qualities.label: A title that tells
qualities.text: The title should point at the premise or the emotional promise, not hide it.

examples.text: A man who built a career on a forged degree must go back and genuinely earn it — the shortcut-taker is forced to take the long road. The contradiction does the selling.

examples.function: A constraint that creates the stakes
examples.text: One night, one reunion, twenty-two years: the premise carries its own clock, and the logline only has to name it.

logline.template: WHEN [an event the protagonist cannot ignore], a [protagonist defined by the trait the story will test] must [goal] or [concrete loss] — and the title should hint at the contradiction.
checklist: Is there an irony or contradiction in your one-line premise?
Can a listener picture the film from the logline alone?
Does it name a goal and what is lost if the goal fails?
Does the title tell an audience what kind of film this is?
Have you tested the logline on someone who knows nothing about the project?

genres.title: Ten story genres
genres.intro: This way of sorting films ignores surface labels like ‘thriller’ or ‘romance’ and groups stories by the engine underneath. Two films that look unrelated can turn out to run on the same engine, and that is the useful part: when you know your engine, you can study every film that shares it. The names below are the widely used ones; the explanations and the examples are ours. Some Indian films sit across two engines, and the interval often marks the switch.

items.label: Monster in the House
items.engine: A deadly force is loose inside a bounded space or community, and somebody’s earlier wrong usually let it in. The tension comes from confinement: running away is not a real option, so the characters must face it.
keys: a threat with a near-mythic quality
a confined world
a sin or mistake that invited the threat

example.text: A predator moves inside a small community of schoolchildren and families, and the people charged with protecting it cannot simply leave.

items.label: Golden Fleece
items.engine: A journey toward a prize, in which the real reward turns out to be what the hero learns about themselves along the way. Companions gather, obstacles arrive in stages, and the road changes the traveller.
keys: a road or a quest
a team assembled along the way
a prize that matters less than the change

example.text: A long, staged pursuit of a seemingly impossible goal, in which allies are gathered and the hero is changed by what the pursuit costs.

items.label: Out of the Bottle
items.engine: A wish is granted, or a curse arrives, by some exceptional means, and the hero must learn what it was really for. The pleasure is the borrowed power; the meaning is the lesson that has to be learned before it is taken back.
keys: a granted wish or a deserved curse
a lesson the hero must learn
a return to ordinary life, changed

example.text: No title on our shelves is literal fantasy, so this is the nearest fit: a shortcut hands the protagonist the life he wanted, and the story is about the price that falls due before he can keep it honestly.

items.label: Dude with a Problem
items.engine: An ordinary person is dropped into extraordinary trouble with no warning and no preparation. The audience identifies because the hero is like them, and the drama is survival through ingenuity rather than special skill.
keys: an innocent hero
a sudden, overwhelming problem
a life-or-death battle against long odds

example.text: Ordinary working men are swept into a machinery of power they did nothing to provoke, and the story becomes whether they can survive it.

items.label: Rites of Passage
items.engine: A life stage — growing up, a loss, a turning age, an addiction, a separation — hurts, and the hero fights it before accepting it. The antagonist is often life itself, and the victory is acceptance or growth.
keys: a life problem everyone recognises
a wrong way of coping first
acceptance as the resolution

example.text: Two children’s small, fierce desire becomes a lesson in how the world sorts people, seen from their height and at their pace.

items.label: Buddy Love
items.engine: Two people who complete each other are brought together, pulled apart and must decide whether they belong together. It covers love stories and friendships alike; the relationship is the plot.
keys: an incomplete hero
the person who completes them
a complication that keeps them apart

example.text: Two former classmates are given one night together, and every complication is the life each has lived since; the relationship is the whole story.

items.label: Whydunit
items.engine: An investigation in which the question is not only who did it but why, and in which the answer exposes something dark about people — including, often, the investigator and the audience.
keys: a detective, official or not
a secret
a dark turn that reflects back on the seeker

example.text: A methodical hunt for a killer whose logic must be understood before it can be predicted, run through an investigator whose own fears are also on trial.

items.label: The Fool Triumphant
items.engine: An underdog everyone dismisses — the establishment above all — turns out to be wiser or stronger than those who mock them. Comedy and satire live here, because the fool exposes the pretensions of the powerful.
keys: an underestimated hero
an establishment that dismisses them
a transformation of how the world sees them

example.text: A small-town man whom the system treats as a joke turns his strangeness into a mirror held up to the people and institutions that dismiss him.

items.label: Institutionalized
items.engine: A group, a family, a gang, a force or a workplace demands loyalty, and the story weighs the comfort of belonging against the cost of losing oneself. Often a newcomer or a doubter shows us the group’s rules.
keys: a group with its own code
a choice between the group and the self
a sacrifice, by the group or by the individual

example.text: A young man is drawn into the codes and loyalties of a crime world, and the question is what belonging will cost him.

items.label: Superhero
items.engine: The reverse of the ordinary person in trouble: an extraordinary figure in an ordinary world that cannot fully understand or accept them. The drama is the burden of being different and the resentment it draws.
keys: a power, gift or destiny
a world that resents or misunderstands it
a cost the hero carries alone

example.text: A man set apart by his capacity and anger carries his village’s fate, and the story weighs that burden against what the world will let him be.

beats.title: The fifteen beats
beats.intro: A beat sheet is a list of moments a feature reliably needs, each with a job and an approximate position. The beat names below are the widely used ones; the page numbers are for a script of about 110 pages and should be scaled for your length. Every explanation and every film mapping is ours. Indian features with an interval often put the Midpoint, or a bigger reversal, at the break, and stretch the second half; the mappings note it where it matters.

items.label: Opening Image
items.purpose: A single snapshot of the hero and their world before the story changes them. It sets tone, and it creates the ‘before’ picture the ending will be measured against.
items.how: Write one vivid, specific image or short scene that shows the hero’s problem in action without explaining it. Ask what the final image will be, and design this one as its opposite.

film.text: Opens on the protagonist’s working solitude rather than on romance: the ‘before’ is a man with no story, so the later emotion has a baseline.

items.label: Theme Stated
items.purpose: Early on, somebody — usually not the hero — raises the question the film is really about, often casually, often without the hero understanding it yet.
items.how: Let a secondary character pose the story’s central question or lesson in passing. Do not underline it; the audience should only recognise it in hindsight.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: Early on, the idea that results are never the only thing being audited is in the air while the protagonist confidently believes the opposite.

items.label: Set-Up
items.purpose: Introduce the hero’s everyday life, the people around them, and every flaw or need the story will work on. Plant what will matter later.
items.how: Show the hero in their home, work and relationships, and make visible what is missing. List the habits and problems that will be tested, and give each a moment on the page.

film.name: Por Thozhil
film.text: Establishes the investigative machinery as competent and routine, and the trainee as the least steady thing in it.

items.label: Catalyst
items.purpose: The event that knocks the hero’s world off its axis — news, an arrival, a loss, an offer. After this, life cannot simply continue as before.
items.how: Make it specific and visible, an event that happens to the hero rather than a mood. It need not be dramatic, but it must be unavoidable.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: Recognition: the one man who can prove the forgery identifies the protagonist, and from that moment the film has a clock and a creditor.

items.label: Debate
items.purpose: The hero hesitates. Should I? Can I? What will it cost? This section lets the audience feel the size of the decision.
items.how: Dramatise doubt through action — attempts to avoid the problem, conversations that weigh the options, a last look at the old life. Keep it moving; debate is not stasis.

film.name: Por Thozhil
film.text: The trainee’s fear works as the hesitation: every early step of the case doubles as a question of whether he can stay in the work at all.

items.label: Break into Two
items.purpose: The hero chooses to enter the new world of the story. It must be an active decision, not something that just happens to them.
items.how: Write a clear moment of commitment the hero owns, and make the new world look and feel different from the old one.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: He accepts the terms and re-enters the life he ran from. The commitment is humiliating rather than heroic, which suits the comedy to come.

items.label: B Story
items.purpose: A second storyline, usually a relationship, that carries the theme. It gives the audience a breather from the main plot and often delivers the lesson the hero needs.
items.how: Introduce a character the hero would not have met in the old world, and let their relationship slowly argue the theme.

film.name: Vikram Vedha
film.text: The officer’s home life carries a quieter thread about applying a principle without flinching, which mirrors the main argument.

items.label: Fun and Games
items.purpose: The promise of the premise is delivered: the scenes the trailer would be cut from. The hero explores the new world, succeeding or failing in ways only this story allows.
items.how: List the set pieces your premise promises and put them here. The stakes are lower than they will become; the audience is enjoying the concept.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: The return to the old institution plays for comedy: the shortcut-taker struggling inside the system he once beat is exactly what the premise sold.

items.label: Midpoint
items.purpose: The story turns. Either a false victory (the hero seems to have won) or a false defeat (all seems lost too early). Stakes rise and the clock often starts.
items.how: Change the direction or the meaning of the hero’s pursuit. Raise the stakes, introduce a deadline, or move from reacting to acting. In an interval film this is often the break.

film.name: Vikram Vedha
film.text: A second story lands and the investigation reverses: the officer begins to audit his own record instead of his target’s.

items.label: Bad Guys Close In
items.purpose: Pressure tightens from outside and inside. External enemies regroup, and the hero’s own team or flaws begin to work against them.
items.how: Escalate opposition steadily and let internal doubts or divisions grow at the same time. Remove allies, resources or certainties one by one.

film.name: Por Thozhil
film.text: The shape of the case collapses and has to be rebuilt, while the trainee’s standing and the partnership come under strain.

items.label: All Is Lost
items.purpose: The lowest point: the opposite of the Midpoint’s position. Often something or someone dies, literally or symbolically, and the old self or old way ends.
items.how: Make the loss concrete and visible. Ask what single blow would make the hero’s goal look impossible, and deliver it.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: The low point is an accounting rather than an exposure: he is shown the bill, and it was paid by somebody who never took the shortcut.

items.label: Dark Night of the Soul
items.purpose: The hero absorbs the loss. This is the moment of despair, reflection and, finally, the beginning of understanding.
items.how: Give the hero a quiet, emotional stretch to feel the full weight of what happened. Let the theme surface in their mind or through the B story.

film.text: The facts of the elapsed years are stated, not dramatised; nothing is destroyed, it is simply established that it is too late, and the characters sit inside that.

items.label: Break into Three
items.purpose: A solution appears, usually by combining what the hero learned in the main story with what the B story taught them. The hero chooses to act.
items.how: Show the insight that unites the two storylines, and let the hero commit to a new plan that only the changed person could make.

film.name: Por Thozhil
film.text: The trainee has to reason the case through alone, without the partner he has been borrowing courage from — the change that makes the ending possible.

items.label: Finale
items.purpose: The hero applies the lesson and confronts the problem. The old world is changed or replaced, and the flaw is overcome or paid for.
items.how: Let the climax turn on the hero’s own choice, informed by the theme. Tie up the B story. Make the resolution cost something.

film.name: Dragon
film.text: He is not caught; he chooses the loss. Routing the ending through a voluntary act gives the theme, not the plot mechanism, the last word.

items.label: Final Image
items.purpose: The ‘after’ picture, the mirror of the Opening Image, showing how much has changed.
items.how: Design it alongside the opening image. The contrast between the two should state the story’s change without a word of explanation.

film.name: Vikram Vedha
film.text: The ending declines to arbitrate and closes on the officer’s choice rather than a verdict, against an opening that invited the audience to approve of his certainty.

checklist: Is your Catalyst an event, specific and visible, in the first eighth of the script?
Is Break into Two an active decision by the hero?
Does your Midpoint change direction or raise stakes, and is it clearly a false victory or a false defeat?
Is All Is Lost a concrete loss, the opposite of the Midpoint?
Do the Opening and Final Images mirror each other?

board.title: The Board
paragraphs: The Board is a physical or digital wall divided into four horizontal rows, on which the whole film is laid out as index cards before a page is drafted. Each row is roughly a quarter of the script: the first runs from the opening to the Break into Two, the second from there to the Midpoint, the third from the Midpoint to the Break into Three, and the fourth through the Finale. About ten cards per row, forty in all, is the usual target for a feature; many more suggests scenes that should merge, many fewer suggests a thin story.

Each card is one scene or a short sequence. Its point is not to hold the scene’s detail but to make the scene’s function visible, so that you can see at a glance where the story sags, repeats itself or skips a step. Because cards can be moved, cut and replaced in seconds, the Board is where structural problems are cheapest to fix. A problem solved on cards costs minutes; the same problem solved in pages costs weeks.

A useful habit is to mark two things on every card. First, the emotional change: does the scene move the hero’s situation from good to bad, or bad to good? Show it with a plus-to-minus or minus-to-plus mark. Second, the conflict: who wants what in the scene, and who or what is in the way? A card with no change or no conflict is a card you should question.

rows.label: Row 1
rows.beats: Opening Image · Theme Stated · Set-Up · Catalyst · Debate · Break into Two

rows.label: Row 2
rows.beats: B Story · Fun and Games · Midpoint

rows.label: Row 3
rows.beats: Bad Guys Close In · All Is Lost · Dark Night of the Soul · Break into Three

card.label: Heading
card.text: Where and when: INT./EXT., location, time of day.

card.label: One line
card.text: What happens, in a single sentence of action.

card.label: Change
card.text: +/− or −/+ for the emotional shift across the scene.

card.label: Conflict
card.text: Who wants what, and what stands in their way.

card.label: Beat
card.text: Which of the fifteen beats this card serves, if any.

steps: Put the beat cards up first, in their rows, as signposts: the Catalyst, the Break into Two, the Midpoint, All Is Lost, the Break into Three.
Fill the scenes you already know, wherever they belong. Leave gaps empty rather than inventing filler.
Look along each row for stretches with no emotional change or no conflict, and fix them on the card before writing.
Colour-code storylines (A story, B story, others) so you can see whether the B story disappears for too long.
Read the Board out loud from first card to last as if pitching the film; wherever you stumble, the structure is weak.
Only when the whole Board holds together, start drafting pages from it.
board.studio: The Story stage’s Beat Sheet already works like a digital board: pick Save the Cat! as the beat sheet and each beat becomes a column of steps you can add, reorder and move between beats.

rules.title: Rules of thumb
rules.intro: The book is remembered for a set of short, catchily named warnings. The names are widely used in screenwriting circles and are kept here as labels; each principle is re-expressed in our own words, with an example of the principle in action from our films.

items.label: Save the Cat
items.principle: Give the audience a reason to side with your hero early, through an action rather than a description. A small act of decency, wit or courage — or simply an undeserved wrong done to them — buys loyalty that lasts through the hero’s worse moments. It matters most for heroes who are difficult or morally grey.

example.text: The trainee’s visible, honest fear wins sympathy in place of a heroic gesture: the audience sides with him because his weakness is recognisable.

items.label: The Pope in the Pool
items.principle: When a scene has to deliver exposition, set it inside something that holds attention on its own — conflict, comedy, danger or a striking image — so the information slips in while the audience is watching something else.

example.text: Exposition arrives as an attack: information about the past is delivered as moves in a contest between two men, so the audience absorbs it while following the duel.

items.label: Double Mumbo Jumbo
items.principle: An audience will accept one leap of faith per story: one impossible premise, one unlikely coincidence, one strange rule. Ask it to accept two unrelated leaps and belief collapses. Choose your one and build everything else on solid ground.

example.text: The film asks the audience to accept a single premise — the forgery and the one man who can expose it — and keeps everything after that grounded in consequence.

items.label: Laying Pipe
items.principle: Too much set-up before the story starts loses the audience. If it takes a long time to explain the world and its rules before the real story begins, the concept may be too complicated, or the explanation should be woven into later scenes.

example.text: The opening spends its time on the protagonist’s present life, not on explaining the past; the history arrives inside the reunion, when the audience already wants it.

items.label: Black Vet
items.principle: Do not pile extra gimmicks onto an idea that already works. Adding one more twist, one more quirk, one more layer can bury a strong concept. Know which element is the hook and let it be the hook.

example.text: The film subtracts rather than adds: no romance subplot or spectacle is layered over the investigation, so the core pressure stays legible.

items.label: Watch Out for That Glacier!
items.principle: Danger must be present and close. A threat that moves slowly or stays far away cannot grip an audience; bring it near, make it personal and make it act soon, or the suspense evaporates.

example.text: The killer’s pattern means the next victim is always a near and specific prospect, so the threat is never distant.

items.label: The Covenant of the Arc
items.principle: Everyone in the story who matters should change, not only the hero. Supporting characters who stay exactly the same make the world feel static; give each of them a small arc of their own.

example.text: The veteran partner is changed by the case too, his armour of detachment tested alongside the trainee’s fear.

items.label: Keep the Press Out
items.principle: Keep the story’s secret contained among the characters who are living it. Once the wider world is told — the media, the authorities, the public at large — the story’s reality and intimacy tend to break. Contain the problem and the audience stays inside it.

example.text: The contest stays between a small circle of people, which keeps the moral argument close and personal rather than public.

studio.title: Use it in the studio
studio.text: Save the Cat! is one of the beat sheets on the Story stage. Open the Beat Sheet, choose Save the Cat! in the picker, and your step outline is laid out under these fifteen beats. Switching beat sheets later is only a view change: your steps keep the beat they were written under.
